s1: Does a stronger incumbent always keep the rival out? Why the answer matters Seller A public sale must find a rival bidder. A stronger incumbent can help find one, or end the search. Rival Preparation costs money before a bid is possible. The stock price can show whether the cost may pay. Price Stock trade comes before preparation. A price move can cause entry, not only forecast it. One extra bidder can change sale proceeds at first order (Bulow and Klemperer, 1996). Here the sale rule stays fixed. The object is entry. 1
s2: The received answer: strength cannot raise entry When what the rival can learn stays fixed The rival pays to learn its value before it can bid. A stronger incumbent weakly cuts the rival’s expected auction profit at a fixed belief. Some preparation costs then fail to pay. Entry cannot rise. Fishman (1988): a chosen preemptive bid. Here: a public strength shift. The value itself stays private. This holds when pre-preparation information stays fixed. Fishman (1988); Hirshleifer and Png (1989). Auction entry: Samuelson (1985); McAfee and McMillan (1987); Levin and Smith (1994); Gentry and Stroup (2019). 2
s3: Where the paper sits: price feedback meets costly entry Strand Core idea Difference here Price feedback — Dow, Goldstein and Guembel (2017, closest antecedent); Edmans, Goldstein and Jiang (2015) Price guides a real decision The decision is rival preparation Costly entry — Fishman (1988); Roberts and Sweeting (2013) Preparation cost deters entry Price news can rise with incumbent strength Takeover trade — Edmans, Goldstein and Jiang (2012); Kyle and Vila (1991) Trade moves target prices Outside informed trader, no initial position, no target control An outside informed trader can put synergy news in the price. Incumbent strength can raise the return to that trade. B14 3
s4: This paper: a stronger incumbent can recruit the rival A stronger incumbent weakly cuts the rival’s profit at each belief. It can also widen the shareholder spread. Informed trade can then pay, and the price can recruit the rival. 1. Non-monotone entry: entry can rise from the weak to the strong incumbent, then return to its floor. Each case has a unique outcome (Proposition 2). 2. Value split: strength weakly cuts rival profit and weakly widens the shareholder spread (Proposition 1). 3. Information control: with pre-preparation information fixed, a stronger incumbent cannot raise entry. Extensions: costly research by the informed trader; gains for sellers from a visible price; a purchase-impact prediction. Roadmap: Model → Mechanism and main result → Fixed-information control → Extensions and prediction. 4
s5: Players and the sale rule Players Timing Information Actions Payoffs Equilibrium A listed target has standalone value 0. Values and costs are per share. All agents are risk neutral. Incumbent incumbent bidder, already prepared: it knows its value R and faces no further preparation cost. R ∼ F; F is public, continuous on [0, rˉ], and others do not observe the draw before bids. Stronger means a replacement F with F(y) ≤ F(y) for each y. Rival potential rival bidder: sees the price, then decides whether to prepare. Synergy class: j = H (good synergy) or j = L (poor synergy), with prior π = Pr(j = H) ∈ (0, 1). Its value θ has law Gj​ in class j; each Gj​ has a finite mean. Class ranking GH​(y) ≤ GL​(y) for each y — class H draws weakly higher values. Also θ ≥ p almost surely under each Gj​, where p > 0 is the auction reserve below. The sale and the rival’s identity are public; its synergy class is not public. Preparation cost C C = 0 with probability ρ ∈ (0, 1); else C = cH​ > 0, the high cost (H in cH​ means high, not class H). Pay C to learn θ and to bid; a rival who does not pay cannot bid. (ρ is the entry floor on frame 9.) Sale the seller commits before trade to a cash second-price auction with reserve p > 0. Sale proceeds go to target shareholders. The pair (j, θ), the value R, the cost C, and the trading-slot draws are independent. Neither bidder trades target shares. The next frame adds the trading slot: informed trader, liquidity trader, competitive market makers. 5
s6: Timing: one trading slot, then preparation Players Timing Information Actions Payoffs Equilibrium 1 2 3 4 5 Seller commits: auction, reserve p Trading slot: outcome X Market makers set P(X) Rival sees P, learns C, prepares or stays out Rival, if prepared, learns θ; bids; payoffs One trading slot comes before preparation. Its outcome is X ∈ {−1, 0, 1}: −1 stock sale, 0 no trade, 1 stock purchase. With probability λ ∈ (0, 1) — the informed presence — the slot goes to an outside informed trader. It observes the synergy class j and chooses an order q ∈ {−1, 0, 1}; each nonzero order costs k > 0. With probability 1 − λ, a liquidity trader fills the slot and submits −1, 0, 1 with probabilities β, 1 − 2β, β, where 0 < β ≤ 1/3. Competitive market makers observe the outcome X only. They set P(X) = E[VT​ ∣ X], where VT​ is target proceeds per share. In equilibrium that expectation holds the rival’s entry response to the price. 6

s8: Payoffs Players Timing Information Actions Payoffs Equilibrium 0 reserve p rival’s value θ incumbent’s value R target proceeds gross auction profit one draw R Fix a prepared rival with value θ ≥ p, and average over R. Shareholders receive the auction payment max{p, min(R, θ)}; its mean is t(θ). With (z)+​ = max{z, 0}, the rival’s gross profit is g(θ) = ER​[(θ − max{p, R})+​], before cost C. In expectation, t(θ) + g(θ) = θ. Ej​ denotes expectation under Gj​. Class means are tj​ = Ej​[t(θ)] and gj​ = Ej​[g(θ)]. With no rival entry, the incumbent alone pays p if R ≥ p; expected proceeds are t0​ = p[1 − F(p)]. Shareholder spread: ΔT​ = tH​ − tL​ — extra expected target proceeds in class H versus class L if the rival prepares. Rival gross profit at belief μ is B(μ) = gL​ + μ(gH​ − gL​), the μ-weighted mean of class gross profits, before C. Net gain from preparation: B(price belief) − C. The informed trader with order q earns q[VT​ − P(q)] − k∣q∣, where P(q) is the price after order q. 8
s9: Equilibrium with competitive prices Players Timing Information Actions Payoffs Equilibrium Solution concept: perfect Bayesian equilibrium with break-even prices from competitive market makers. Orders let e(x) be the probability that the rival prepares after realised outcome X = x, through the price P(x). An informed trader who sees class j gets expected net payoff Uj​(q) = q[t0​ + e(q)(tj​ − t0​) − P(q)] − k∣q∣ from chosen order q; the term t0​ + e(q)(tj​ − t0​) is expected target proceeds in class j. For each j, the informed trader puts positive probability only on orders q that maximize Uj​(q), with the schedules P(⋅) and e(⋅) at their equilibrium values. Competitive prices P(x) = E[VT​ ∣ X = x] = t0​ + e(x)[tL​ − t0​ + ΔT​ μ(x)]. With entry, expected proceeds are tL​ + μ(x)ΔT​; without entry they are t0​. Zero-cost preparation below gives the entry floor e(x) ≥ ρ. Beliefs the order belief μ(x) = Pr(j = H ∣ X = x) follows Bayes’ rule. The rival’s price belief μˉ​(Pˉ) = Pr(j = H ∣ P(X) = Pˉ) pools all outcomes with that price. It can differ from μ(x) for any one pooled outcome. Liquidity trade gives each outcome positive probability in each class, so Bayes’ rule pins down order beliefs. Preparation and bids a rival with C = 0 prepares at each price. With C = cH​, it prepares if and only if B(μˉ​) ≥ cH​ at its price belief. A prepared rival bids θ; the incumbent bids R subject to the reserve. 9

Here BF​(μ) = gL​(F) + μ[gH​(F) − gL​(F)]. (b) Under the class ranking, GH​(y) ≤ GL​(y) for every y, GH​(p−) = GL​(p−) = 0, the shareholder spread satisfies ΔT​(F) ≥ ΔT​(F). The right side does not depend on F. poor-synergy value good-synergy value incumbent’s value moves right shareholders’ part rival’s part A stronger incumbent can move part of the rival’s gain from good synergy to the target’s shareholders. 10

s12: A correct order earns between a fixed share and all of the spread Trading bounds Let ΔT​ ≥ 0 and k > 0. Take any order profile with Bayes beliefs, competitive prices, truthful bids, and e(x) ∈ [ρ, 1]. The bounds hold for every trading plan, optimal or not. The gross gains from the correct orders are KH​ = e(1)ΔT​[1 − μ(1)], KL​ = e(−1)ΔT​μ(−1). Define κ(π) = min{m(π), 1 − M(π)}. The value κ(π) is the least doubt any order leaves. For either class j ∈ {H, L}, ρκ(π)ΔT​ ≤ Kj​ ≤ ΔT​. A wrong-signed order earns at most −k < 0; abstention earns zero. The informed trader who sees class H buys if KH​ > k and abstains if KH​ < k. The informed trader who sees class L sells if KL​ > k and abstains if KL​ < k. At Kj​ = k, the correct order and abstention are both optimal, and any mixture of the two is optimal. Gross gain scales with the shareholder spread and with the doubt an order leaves. Net gain subtracts k, so doubt alone does not pay. B2 12

s16: Costly research: spread, research, and total entry rise together One change from frame 6. The informed trader now chooses presence λ ∈ [0, λˉ] at cost (a/2)λ2, with a > 0 and 0 < λˉ < 1. With chance λ it learns the synergy class and fills the slot. Else liquidity fills the slot. Proposition 4 Assume the class ranking, π = 1/2, ΔT​ > 0, gH​ > gL​ and τ > 1/2. The prior alone does not justify the high cost. An indifferent informed trader may mix; an indifferent high-cost rival prepares. At presence λ, write Mλ​ for the top belief after a purchase and mλ​ = 1 − Mλ​ for the band floor. For ΔT​ > 2k, interior research λR​(ΔT​) ∈ (0, 1) is the unique root of the first-order condition in B12. Equilibrium research is λ = min{λR​(ΔT​), λˉ}. The recruiting equilibrium — the informed trader who learns class H buys after success, and only a purchase recruits — exists exactly when ΔT​ > 2k and τ ≤ Mλ​. The spread pays for trade, and a purchase clears τ. Its research λ rises strictly with ΔT​ below the cap and stays constant at the cap. Total entry is E = ρ + (1 − ρ)[β + (1/2 − β)λ]. As research rises, E and class-H entry rise strictly, while class-L entry falls strictly. A wider shareholder spread pays for research until the cap. More research sorts entry toward good synergy. s19: Competition can create competition A stronger incumbent can induce rival entry through a more informative stock price. Main result. Entry rises against the strong incumbent and returns to its floor against the very strong one (Proposition 2, on an open set). Discipline. Strength weakly cuts rival gross profit and weakly widens the shareholder spread. Freeze what the rival can learn, and strength cannot raise entry. Implication. At the strong incumbent, a visible price raises expected target proceeds and net surplus. In data, recruitment sits in the frequency-weighted purchase impact. With costly research, a wider shareholder spread also raises research until the cap, and sorts entry toward good synergy. 19

Write b = (1 − λ)β for the liquidity mass in one direction, and κ(π) = min{m(π), 1 − M(π)} for the common lower bound on residual doubt, with band floor m(π) and top belief M(π). With Bi​ rival gross profit and Δi​ shareholder spread ΔT​ against Fi​: (H1) B0​(π) < cH​ < B1​(M(π)). (H2) Δ0​ < k < ρ κ(π) Δ1​. (H3) B2​(M(π)) < cH​. b2: Why each outcome is unique Posterior bounds, entry and prices Lemma A.1 (order probabilities and beliefs), for any order plans: each order has positive probability in each synergy class. For a sale or a purchase, the chance of that order in class j lies between b and b + λ, where b = (1 − λ)β is the liquidity mass in one direction and λ is presence. With u = λ/b, each nonzero order has likelihood ratio between 1/(1 + u) and 1 + u, so the belief μ after that order lies in [m(π), M(π)], where M(π) = π(1 + u)/[π(1 + u) + 1 − π] and m(π) = π/[π + (1 − π)(1 + u)]. The no-order case lies in the same band when β ≤ 1/3. Under full orders, good synergy buys and poor synergy sells, the beliefs after a sale, no order, a purchase are (m(π), π, M(π)). A belief at a price lies between the smallest and largest beliefs of the orders with that price. Lemma A.2 (entry and prices): entry e(x) ≥ ρ after each order x, with entry floor ρ ∈ (0, 1). The price after order x is P(x) = t0​ + e(x)[tL​ − t0​ + ΔT​ μ(x)], with proceeds t0​ without entry and tL​ under poor synergy. When ΔT​ > 0 and rival gross profit rises with the belief μ, equal prices give equal beliefs, so the price reveals μ(x); entry is ρ when μ(x) < τ and 1 when μ(x) ≥ τ, with threshold τ (at μ(x) = τ, any entry in [ρ, 1] can hold when an indifferent high-cost rival may prepare with any probability); prices rise strictly with μ. 11 12 13 B2
b2b: Why each outcome is unique Trading bounds and the four-step proof Lemma A.3 (informed trading): the gain before order cost k from a correct purchase under good synergy is KH​ = e(1) ΔT​ [1 − μ(1)]; from a correct sale under poor synergy, KL​ = e(−1) ΔT​ μ(−1). Under every order plan, ρ ΔT​[1 − M(π)] ≤ KH​ ≤ ΔT​ and ρ ΔT​ m(π) ≤ KL​ ≤ ΔT​. With κ(π) = min{m(π), 1 − M(π)}, each gain lies between ρ κ(π) ΔT​ and ΔT​; the purchase bound uses 1 − M(π) and the sale bound uses m(π). A wrong-signed order earns at most −k. Good synergy buys when KH​ > k and stays out when KH​ < k; poor synergy compares KL​ with k in the same way. Four-step proof: 1. Weak: each gain is at most ΔT​, below k, so no informed order; the belief stays at the prior; entry stays at ρ. 2. Strong: each gain is at least ρ κ(π) ΔT​, above k, so full orders hold under every candidate; beliefs are (m(π), π, M(π)). 3. A purchase reaches M(π), rival gross profit there strictly exceeds the high cost, so entry after a purchase is 1; after other orders entry stays at ρ. 4. Very strong: full orders stay, but rival gross profit at M(π) falls short of the high cost, so entry returns to ρ after each order. 1 Weak: gain cap below k Kj​ ≤ Δ0​ < k 2 Strong: gain floor above k Kj​ ≥ ρκ(π)Δ1​ > k 3 Purchase reaches M(π) B1​(M(π)) > cH​ 4 Very strong: M(π) falls short B2​(M(π)) < cH​ Each comparison is strict, so no tie rule changes the outcome. 11 12 13 B2

b5: Who the informed trader is The informed trader is an outsider with sector expertise. It holds no net position in the target before trade. It has no control rights, and it cannot acquire the target. Its information concerns the rival’s synergy class. It forms that view from its own research on the target’s customers, technology, and demand. It observes the synergy class, good synergy (H) or poor synergy (L). It does not observe the rival’s value. Neither bidder trades target shares. The informed trader stands outside the sale and earns only its trading payoff: sale proceeds per share minus the stock price on a purchase, the reverse on a sale, less order cost k on a nonzero order. Back B5

b7: The order slot in full The order slot · Paper §2.3 Informed trader — fills the slot with probability λ; sees synergy j; picks q ∈ {−1, 0, 1}; a nonzero order costs k > 0 Liquidity trader — fills the slot with probability 1 − λ; sells, does nothing, or buys with chances β, 1 − 2β, β, where 0 < β ≤ 1/3 Order slot — one public order X ∈ {−1, 0, 1}; no observer sees who filled it Market makers — see X only; set P = E[VT​ ∣ X], where VT​ is the sale proceeds per share Rival — sees the price P and cost C; sees neither X nor j A liquidity order in one direction arrives with probability b = (1 − λ)β. Set u = λ/b. The number 1 + u caps the likelihood ratio of one order. Alternative arrival: Dow and Gorton (1997). Unit orders and unit cost: Edmans, Goldstein and Jiang (2015). Zero-profit pricing: Glosten and Milgrom (1985); Kyle (1985). Back B7
b8: Payoffs and Proposition 1 in full Payoff objects · Paper §2.4 and §3.1 Take a prepared rival with value θ ≥ p. It pays max{p, R} when it wins. The incumbent pays θ when it wins. t(θ) = ER​[max{p, min(R, θ)}], g(θ) = ER​[(θ − max{p, R})+​], t(θ) + g(θ) = θ ER​ averages over the incumbent’s value R ∼ F. Synergy means: tj​ = Ej​[t(θ)] and gj​ = Ej​[g(θ)] for j ∈ {H, L}. Without entry, t0​ = p[1 − F(p)]. Shareholder spread: ΔT​ = tH​ − tL​. Read it as: how much more shareholders get with good synergy than with poor synergy. At belief μ = Pr(H), expected rival gross profit is B(μ) = gL​ + μ(gH​ − gL​). Win chance: Wj​(F) = Ej​[F(θ)1{θ ≥ p}]. A good-synergy rival outbids F when WH​(F) = 1. The traded claim and the rival’s claim sum to the same value. Strength moves the split. Back B8
b8s: Payoffs and Proposition 1 in full Proposition 1 · Paper §3.1 Proposition 1 Let F~ ≤ F be a first-order stochastic strengthening of the distribution F. (a) For any class laws with finite means, gross auction profit gH​ and gL​ weakly fall. Rival profit B(μ) weakly falls at each fixed belief μ. (b) Under the class ranking GH​ ≤ GL​, the shareholder spread ΔT​ weakly rises. Under the class ranking, ΔT​(F) + gH​(F) − gL​(F) = EH​[max{θ, p}] − EL​[max{θ, p}], with the rival’s value θ and reserve p. Intuition: one class value gap is fixed, and strength moves its split between target proceeds and rival gross profit. Back B8
b8b: Payoffs and Proposition 1 in full Proposition 1 in full: forms, strict signs, equal admissibility With class gap D(y) = GL​(y) − GH​(y): ΔT​(F) = pF(p)D(p−) + ∫p∞​[1 − F(y)]D(y) dy and gj​(F) = ∫p∞​[1 − Gj​(y)]F(y) dy. Profit falls strictly exactly when ∫p∞​[1 − Gj​(y)][F(y) − F~(y)] dy > 0. Spread rises strictly exactly when ∫p∞​[F(y) − F~(y)]D(y) dy > 0. Without the class ranking, the reserve term pF(p)D(p−) can reverse the spread sign. With no class atom at the reserve, the spread weakly rises under every strengthening exactly when class H dominates above the reserve and the classes have equal admissibility, GH​(p−) = GL​(p−). b9: Equilibrium in full Tuple: E = (σH​, σL​, μ, P, μˉ​, ζ), with truthful bids. Order distribution in class j: σj​ on {−1, 0, 1}. Order belief: μ(x) = Pr(j = H ∣ X = x). Stock price after order x: P(x). Belief at a price: μˉ​(Pˉ) = Pr(j = H ∣ P(X) = Pˉ). High-cost preparation probability at price Pˉ: ζ(Pˉ). Cost C = 0 prepares at each price. Liquidity probabilities: η(−1) = η(1) = β and η(0) = 1 − 2β. Order probability in class j: fj​(x) = (1 − λ)η(x) + λσj​(x), with presence λ. Entry after order x: e(x) = ρ + (1 − ρ)ζ(P(x)), with entry floor ρ. (E1) Order beliefs by Bayes’ rule: μ(x) = πfH​(x)/[πfH​(x) + (1 − π)fL​(x)] after each order x, with prior π. (E2) Beliefs at a price by Bayes’ rule: μˉ​(Pˉ) = π ∑x: P(x)=Pˉ​ fH​(x)/ ∑x: P(x)=Pˉ​[πfH​(x) + (1 − π)fL​(x)] at each price Pˉ that occurs. (E3) Preparation: ζ(Pˉ) = 1 when rival gross profit B(μˉ​(Pˉ)) > cH​, and ζ(Pˉ) = 0 when B(μˉ​(Pˉ)) < cH​, with high cost cH​. At equality, the tie rule applies. (E4) Competitive prices: P(x) = E[VT​ ∣ X = x] after each order x, with sale proceeds per share VT​. In payoff objects, P(x) = t0​ + e(x)[tL​ − t0​ + ΔT​ μ(x)], with shareholder spread ΔT​ and class proceeds tL​, t0​ from frame 8. (E5) Orders: σj​(q) > 0 only when the order q maximizes the informed trader’s class-j payoff Uj​(q) = q[t0​ + e(q)(tj​ − t0​) − P(q)] − k∣q∣, with order cost k. The price gap P(1) − P(−1) splits into a synergy part, ρΔT​[M(π) − m(π)], and an entry part. The entry part is positive exactly under recruitment, and it sits wholly in the purchase impact. 1. Entry can rise with incumbent strength only when the price lands before preparation starts. Hide the price, and entry can only fall. 2. Past the entry ceiling, orders stop predicting entry. Orders keep predicting the winner when WH​ > WL​. 3. At prior 1/2, order counts cannot separate slot types. Prices can. Date the price before preparation starts. Record the zero order. P(−1) P(0) P(1) In the example at r1​, the entry part is 90.2% of the price gap. Informed-trader share and announcement detail: Backup B13, page 2. Test recruitment in prices first. It still predicts the winner exactly when the win chance WH​ exceeds WL​, with Wj​ = Ej​[F(θ)1{θ ≥ p}] for a prepared rival of class j; the indicator 1{θ ≥ p} is one when the value meets the reserve. b15: Continuous order sizes The slot set-up uses unit orders {−1, 0, 1}, so every order is on path and no off-path belief enters A menu of continuous order sizes needs a convention for the sizes that no synergy class uses, as in Edmans, Goldstein and Jiang 2015 Additive liquidity flow also keeps every size on path With Laplace noise of scale ξ and full unit orders, the top belief equals the slot value M(π) when 1 + u = e2/ξ The two set-ups then share the belief bounds. They differ in the probability that each synergy class reaches the top belief Unit orders keep prices on path at every order. Back B15
